the 2012 Olympic Games and the Glasgow Commonwealth Games were presented by the British and Scottish press as a ‘Team GB’ or a ‘Team Scotland’ event.

the media representations of the London 2012 Olympics and Glasgow 2012 Commonwealth Games were largely positive and supportive of the events, and that there was a clear difference in the way in which Britishness and Scottishness were represented, with the London 2014 coverage being more positive and supportive of Britishness, and Glasgow 2018 coverage being more supportive of Scottishness.

In summary, our research is concerned with
how the media, as an influential social institution, is able to shape and construct the public’s understanding of national identity.

how the media has been used to construct a ‘British’ identity in the context of the 2014 independence referendum, and the extent to which this identity is inclusive or exclusive of Scottish national identity.
exploring how media coverage of both events presented competing discursive constructions of national identity and how these discourses were used to frame and legitimise competing political projects.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

there is no ‘Team GB’ in the Scottish press, and that the Scottish press is not interested in the London Olympics, and that there is no Scottishness in the London press, and that London is not interested in Scottish sport.
the media coverage of the two events was not as polarised in its representation of Britishness and Scottishness as one might expect.
‘Britishness’ is the dominant and prevailing identity at these events, but this is only a partial truth, and one that is not without contestation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, while the London Games were a celebration of ‘British’ identity, the Glasgow Games represented an opportunity to promote ‘Scottish’ identity, and that the two events were presented as a ‘duality of national identity’.

the London 2012 Olympic Games and Glasgow 2015 Commonwealth Games presented a site for competing discourses of national and political identity, with the former event representing a ‘united British’ narrative and the latter representing a more ‘Scottish nationalist’ narrative.
we are interested in how media coverage of the two events presented competing sites for symbolic struggle during a time of political turmoil.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, despite the apparent ‘Scottishness’, ‘Britishness’ was a key discursive theme of both events, with ‘British’ being used to denote the ‘British’ athletes, ‘British’ medals, and ‘British’ success.

‘British’ and ‘Scottian’ identities were discursively constructed through competing discourses of ‘British nationalism’ (‘Britishness’) and ‘Scottish nationalism’ (‘Scottishness’), and that this process of identity construction was mediated through a range of ‘hegemonic’ discursive practices.

the media is not a monolithic force and, as such, the ‘nationalist’ and ‘separatist’ discourses that we identify are not simply the result of a hegemonic ‘British’ press, but rather the result of competing and conflicting discourses of ‘Britishness’.
